existing.title: complete_task on a task whose blockers are still open succeeds silently
existing.description: Repro 2026-09-16 09:17 UTC: `tasqx_add_dependency ref=610 depends_on=623` (623 pending) returned blocked:true; then `tasqx_complete_task ref=610` returned status done, unblocked [] — no error, no warning field, nothing in the response saying a blocker was still open. The `unmet_blockers` list on the task is the only trace. Compare: `tasqx_stop_timer` on a pending task and `tasqx_complete_task` on a done task are both `conflict`. If a blocked task can be done, the dependency was wrong or the work jumped the queue; either way the caller should be told. Suggest a `warnings: ["completed with open blockers: #623"]` field on the response at minimum, and an `outcomes` metric ("completed while blocked") so it shows up in the retro data. A refusal with `force:true` opt-out is the stricter alternative.

new.title: complete_task refuses a task with open blockers unless force:true; outcomes counts completed-while-blocked

existing.title: Recurring task spawn copies fields but not the description annotation or checks
existing.description: Repro: #604 "Weekly backlog grooming" (recurrence "weekly on mon", due 2026-09-21, one description annotation, tag chore, est 15m) completed via `tasqx_complete_task` on 2026-09-16 09:17 UTC. The response carried `spawned: {short_id 625, due 2026-09-28}`. `tasqx_get_task 625 view=card` shows title, L, est 15m, tag chore, due, Repeats — and no Description row, no Checks, no Notes. So the next occurrence lost the paragraph explaining what the chore is and how "done" is judged; a session picking #625 up from `tasqx next` gets a bare title. Suggest copying the oldest annotation (the description, by the card convention) and the check bodies (reset to open) onto the spawned task, or linking the spawn to its predecessor (`spawned_from: 604`) so brief_task can pull the predecessor's notes. Also worth a decision: should the spawn carry the predecessor's delivery notes as "last time" context?

new.title: Recurrence spawn copies the description annotation and checks (reset) and records spawned_from

existing.title: tasqx export with a project filter still exports every memory doc and every project in the store
existing.description: Repro: `tasqx export project:ledger > ledger-export.json` (213 KB). Parsed: tasks = 21, all project ledger (the filter worked for tasks and a `dropped_dependencies` key explains cut edges); but `docs` = 41 with projects tasqx 24, unscoped 10, claude-config 4, ledger 2, tasqx-findings 1, and `projects` lists all six projects including the archived ones, and `events` is the full log. So a "give me the ledger project" export carries every other project's knowledge docs, which is both a data-leak risk when the file is shared and a surprise on `tasqx import` into another store. Suggest: with a project filter, export only docs scoped to that project plus (opt-in) unscoped docs, only the matching project rows, and only events for exported tasks; state in the header what was dropped.

new.title: Export honours the project filter for docs, projects and events, and states what was dropped

existing.title: get_task with any explicit annotations_limit drops the byte budget, so one 240KB note blows the tool-output limit
existing.description:
Repro: scratch task #609 carries one 240,000-byte annotation (accepted by `tasqx annotate` in 55 ms, searchable). `tasqx_get_task ref=609 include_json=false annotations_limit=5` returned 240,408 characters and Claude Code refused the result ("exceeds maximum allowed tokens"), saving it to a file. The tool description does say that naming ANY annotations_limit "removes the response's byte budget entirely", but the reason for naming a small limit is precisely to keep the response small, and the default page (omit the parameter) would presumably have included the same note anyway because it is the newest. Also, the markdown view after `tasqx_remove_annotation` shows "Annotations (1)" with no tombstone line, so the audit trail promised in the remove_annotation doc is invisible here.

Suggested: keep the byte budget in force always and truncate individual annotation bodies past N KB with a "(truncated, body_bytes=240000, read with annotations_offset/limit=1)" marker; add a per-annotation `max_body_bytes` param; and consider refusing or warning on annotation bodies over, say, 64 KB at write time since nothing in tasqx can display them. Render the tombstone as "(annotation <id> removed <ts>)" in both views.

new.title: get_task: keep the byte budget with any annotations_limit; truncate oversized bodies with a marker; max_body_bytes

existing.title: Card view drops the Description/Delivered rows when annotations_limit=0 or the first note is paged out
existing.description: Repro: `tasqx_get_task ref=586 view=card include_json=false annotations_limit=0` right after completing #586 (3 annotations). The Description row read "(first note not on this page — re-read with annotations_offset)" and there was no Delivered row at all, even though the task is done and its newest annotation starts with the delivery paragraph. The card is meant for a person, and annotations_limit=0 is the documented way to read fields without history, so the two should not interact: the card should fetch the oldest and newest annotation's first paragraph independently of the annotation page requested. Same risk on a task with more than 20 annotations where the oldest note falls off the default page.

existing.title: No way to correct an annotation in place; the oldest note is the card's Description so a fix reorders it
existing.description: Case: the description annotation on ledger #587 (the oldest note, which the card renders as Description) says `budgets(category_id PRIMARY KEY, month TEXT, limit_cents)`. During implementation the month column was dropped on purpose (a budget applies to every month, per #595). The executor flagged that "#587's description in tasqx still says month" and asked for it to be corrected. There is no `tasqx_update_annotation`; the only options are `tasqx_remove_annotation` (a hard delete, which also makes the next-oldest note become the Description) plus re-adding at the end (which puts the corrected text where the card reads Delivered), or a correction annotation that the card never shows. `tasqx_update_memory` exists for docs with optimistic concurrency; the same shape for annotations (`tasqx_update_annotation id, body, expected_rev`), keeping the original timestamp and position, would close this. Memory search would then also stop ranking the stale sentence.

new.title: Card rows: Description/Delivered independent of annotation paging; update_annotation op; Delivered pinned at completion

existing.title: tracked shows PT0S while a task is active: the running interval is invisible in list, summary and the card
existing.description: Observed with three clocks running (#587 #588 #589, started 09:07-09:11 UTC): `tasqx_list_tasks filter=status:active fields=[tracked,active_since]` returned tracked PT0S for all three at 09:15, `tasqx_summary group_by=status metrics=[tracked_total]` showed active tracked_total PT0S, and `tasqx_get_task 589` said "tracked PT0S (0s)" next to "active since 4 minutes ago". Only on `tasqx_complete_task` did tracked jump to PT3M54S. A reader asking "how long has this been going" has to subtract active_since from now themselves, and a summary of in-flight work under-reports by every open interval. Suggest `tracked` (or a separate `tracked_live`) include the open interval up to the report instant, with the card's Status row reading e.g. "tracked 4m (running)".

new.title: Timers: include the running interval in tracked everywhere; auditable adjust_tracked op (MCP + CLI)

existing.title: No way to correct tracked time: stop_timer cannot be backdated and tracked is not modifiable, so an idle gap poisons calibration
existing.description: Datapoint: ledger #591 started 09:43:40 UTC, its subagent finished at 09:45 (109 s), but a sibling subagent (#593) stalled in a harness watchdog and the planning session was idle from about 09:47 until 12:12 UTC. On completion #591 recorded tracked PT2H29M54S against a 45m estimate; `tasqx_outcomes` calibration for the project moved from a 0.15 median ratio to include a 3.3x overrun that is pure idle time. `tasqx_stop_timer` takes no `at` timestamp, `tasqx_modify_task` lists tracked among the non-modifiable fields, and `tasqx undo` would revert the whole completion. The same problem hits any human who forgets to stop a clock overnight. Suggest: `stop_timer at=<instant>` (bounded by the interval start and now), or a `tasqx_adjust_tracked ref, delta, reason` op recorded as its own event so the correction is auditable, and an `idle_gap` heuristic in outcomes that flags intervals with no annotation, check or token event for more than N minutes.

new.title: Timers: include the running interval in tracked everywhere; auditable adjust_tracked op (MCP + CLI)

existing.title: complete_task has no total_tokens field; agent harnesses often report one number, not an input/output split
existing.description: Claude Code's Agent tool reports a subagent's spend as one number (`subagent_tokens: 21145` for task #586) with no input/output/cache split. `tasqx_complete_task` only has input_tokens, output_tokens, cache_read_tokens, cache_creation_tokens, so the honest options are to put the total under input_tokens (done for #586, which now shows tokens_out 0 and skews any in/out ratio) or to report nothing and lose the datapoint. Suggest a `total_tokens` param (or `tokens` with an explicit `split: unknown`) recorded as its own measurement kind, and have `tasqx_summary`/`tasqx_outcomes` show it as "total (unsplit)". The `fresh_tokens` gauge against budget_tokens should count it too.

existing.title: No MCP or CLI verb to add a token measurement after completion; token.add is reachable only via `tasqx api` and its required fields are discovered one error at a time
existing.description: Repro: #602 was completed before its executor's token count arrived. `tasqx tokens` only has `recompute`; no MCP tool adds a measurement. `tasqx api` works but took four attempts: envelope needs `tasqx:"1"` and `method` (not `op`), then `source` was required, then `confidence`; the final working request was {"tasqx":"1","method":"token.add","params":{"ref":602,"input_tokens":37898,"tool":"claude-code","model":"claude-sonnet-5","source":"self-report","confidence":"medium"}}. Suggest a `tasqx_add_tokens` MCP tool mirroring complete_task's token params, a `tasqx tokens add <ref>` CLI verb, and a single error that lists every missing envelope/param field at once.

existing.title: Tags are case-sensitive in the filter DSL (+upper misses UPPER) and tags with spaces are accepted
existing.description: Repro: `tasqx_tag_task ref=603 tags=["has space","ünïcödé","UPPER","perf"]` was accepted and the tag set came back as ["UPPER","has space","perf","ünïcödé"]. Then `tasqx_list_tasks filter='project:ledger +UPPER'` found #603 but `+upper` returned 0 rows, and `+"has space"` (quoted) matched. Category names in most trackers are case-insensitive; a session that tags `+Bug` and another `+bug` will split the backlog. Either normalise tags to lowercase on write (with a bad_request on whitespace) or make the `+tag` filter case-insensitive. An empty-string tag is already refused with a clear message, so the validation hook exists.

existing.title: tasqx chart subcommands take no filter, so a per-project burndown is impossible
existing.description: Repro: `tasqx chart burndown project:ledger` -> "error: unexpected argument 'project:ledger' found". `tasqx chart --help` lists throughput, heatmap and burndown with no filter option, while `tasqx report`, `tasqx list` and `tasqx agenda` all accept the filter DSL. On a store with 600+ tasks across six projects the global burndown says nothing about the one project being worked. Suggest the same positional filter the other read verbs take, and a `project` param on the equivalent JSON API ops.

existing.title: MCP conflict errors give CLI remedies (tasqx show --json, --expected-rev) instead of MCP tool names
existing.description: Repro via MCP on 2026-09-16: `tasqx_modify_task ref=603 set={estimate:"1.5h",priority:"M"} expected_rev=1` returned `error [conflict]: expected_rev 1 but task is at rev 5: re-read with "tasqx show 603 --json" and retry with --expected-rev 5`. The remedy names the CLI command and a CLI flag; the MCP caller has `tasqx_get_task` and an `expected_rev` parameter. By contrast `tasqx_update_memory` gets it right: "re-read it with tasqx_get_memory and retry with expected_rev 0". Suggest the core error carries a structured remedy (op + field) and each transport renders it in its own vocabulary. Same pattern appears in the `tasqx_add_dependency` not_found message which is fine, and in the memory get error which is fine.

existing.title: MCP add_task stores CLI inline sugar verbatim in the title without a warning field
existing.description: Repro: `tasqx_add_task title="fix crash +bug due:friday project:tasqx !H est:2h" project=tasqx-findings priority=L` stored the title verbatim (task #612, since cancelled). The tool description says it will, and the response echoes the stored title so a caller CAN check, but nothing flags it. An agent that copies a CLI habit into MCP gets a task with no due date, no tags, priority L and a misleading title, silently. Suggest a `warnings: ["title contains inline sugar: +bug, due:friday, project:tasqx, !H, est:2h"]` field on the add_task/modify_task response, or an opt-in `parse_sugar: true`.

existing.title: set_check on a mistyped check id says not_found but does not list the task's real check ids
existing.description: Repro: `tasqx_set_check ref=589 check_id=01a0a971-4afa-741d-ac74-9c9a34d83352 state=passed` (one hex pair mistyped from a 36-char UUID) returned `error [not_found]: task #589 has no check 01a0a971-4afa-741d-ac74-9c9a34d83352`. Recovery needed a full `tasqx_get_task` read. Since a task rarely has more than a handful of checks, the error could list them (`checks on #589: 01a0a971-4afa-… "python3 -m ledger --version …", …`) or accept the check's `position` (0-based, already in the response of add_check) as an alternative key. Same applies to `tasqx_remove_check` and to `tasqx_remove_annotation`, where a typo is a hard delete of the wrong row if it happens to exist.

existing.title: brief_task memory hits include other projects' docs and the task's own description
existing.description:
When `tasqx_brief_task` was called on ledger task #586 (view card, include_json false) the "From memory" section listed 10 of 29 hits. Two problems for the reader about to start work:

1. Cross-project noise: hit 5 was "After a long multi-agent run, trial-merge onto the current main and re-gate before pushing" from source `DESIGN.md §12 D132-D135; merge 0f903c1`, a doc that belongs to the `tasqx` project and has nothing to do with a Python ledger. It matched on generic words from the derived query (probably "readme"). The brief does not say which project a hit belongs to, so the reader cannot tell it is foreign without opening it.

2. Self-echo: hit 1 was the task's own description annotation (`task:#586`), which the card had just printed in full. It costs a slot and adds nothing.

Suggested: scope the derived query to the task's project plus unscoped docs by default (the same `include_unscoped` shape search_memory has), exclude the task's own annotations, and print the project of each hit. Repro: `tasqx_brief_task ref=586 view=card include_json=false` on 2026-09-16 09:00 UTC.

existing.title: Decide (DESIGN.md §12): mcp serve cannot route through a daemon, so agent writes never reach watch or the desktop app live
existing.description: The MCP server runs its own in-process engine and refuses --socket ("not a socket client", D73); a TASQX_SOCK in its environment is ignored without a message. So everything an agent does is invisible to `tasqx watch` and the desktop app until they re-read, while a daemon is running beside it, and two writers share one SQLite file. Decide in DESIGN.md §12: keep D73 and document the trade-off (and warn on an ignored TASQX_SOCK), or let `mcp serve` act as a daemon client when one is reachable. Found in #1101 (F3).

`tasqx agenda` (demo store) writes day headings as `Today · Sun 2026-09-13`, `Tomorrow · Mon 2026-09-14`, `Wed 2026-09-16`, the header as `through 2026-09-27 (+14d)`, and an overdue WHEN cell as `due 2026-09-11`. `tasqx list` over the same rows writes `2d ago`, `today 17:00`, `tomorrow 17:00`, `Wed`, `22 Sep`.

existing.title: watch_reconnect test leaks a "reconnect proof" task into the real store on every run
existing.description: Cause: crates/tasqx-cli/tests/watch_reconnect.rs kills daemon 1 (SIGKILL leaves the stale socket file), spawns daemon 2, and wait_for_socket returns at once because the stale file exists. The `tasqx add "reconnect proof"` subprocess then sets only TASQX_SOCK, connect is refused, and open_backend (backend.rs) falls back in-process against the DEFAULT store, i.e. the developer's real ~/Library/Application Support/dev.tasqx.tasqx/tasks.db. 36 tasks #19-#59 leaked on 2026-09-13, one per cargo test run. Fix: pass TASQX_DB=<temp db> on every subprocess the test spawns, and remove the stale socket before spawning daemon 2 so the wait actually waits. Lesson: any integration test that spawns the tasqx binary must set TASQX_DB, because the in-process fallback is silent when TASQX_SOCK is the only env var; the guard hook only covers cargo run / target/debug/tasqx, not cargo test.

existing.title: Collapse the duplicated table, theme and contrast code in the CLI renderer
existing.description:
The CLI's rendering layer repeats itself: five theme definitions spell out the same seventeen roles, the numeric table is written twice byte-for-byte, fifteen consecutive if-blocks build detail rows one at a time, and the same row-building closure appears six times across two files. None of it is wrong, all of it is more code than the logic needs. This task collapses the repetition into the helpers it is already almost shaped like, roughly 600 lines, without changing a single byte of what reaches a terminal. Done means the rendered output is identical — the existing byte-level regression tests are the proof — and the four gates pass.

Cut list (from the repo-wide ponytail audit, 2026-09-17):
- `theme.rs:664-966` — `builtin()`'s five theme blocks. nord, gruvbox, dracula and solarized repeat one 17-role list differing only in six hexes plus `project`/`tag`/`timer.active`, the ramp is always `[#8a8a8a, warn, danger]`, and mono repeats it again as 100 lines of `StyleSpec{bold:Some(true),..}`. One role template over a 5-row palette table, plus `spec_only_bold`/`spec_only_dim` helpers. ~230 lines.
- `render.rs:2376-2420` — `detail_rows`' fifteen consecutive `if !s(result,"k").is_empty() { row(…) }` blocks. One loop over a `&[(json_key, label, DetailField, Fmt)]` slice. ~90 lines.
- `render.rs:3270-3300` and `:3510-3560` — the numeric-table block written twice: `MIN_KEY`/`MAX_KEY`, `key_w` via `.chain([header])`, per-label `Column::fixed`, then a byte-identical right-aligning closure. One `num_table(ctx, header, labels, rows, total)`. ~60 lines.
- `render.rs:764,913,3044` and `settings.rs:404,562,1242` — six copies of the same row closure (`cells.iter().zip(&w).filter(…).map(…)` into `join_cells`). One `row_cells(ctx, &[usize], cells)` next to `join_cells`. ~45 lines.
- `html.rs:1587-1662` — the contrast stack: `relative_luminance`, `contrast_ratio`, `darkened_for_contrast`, `lightened_for_contrast`, `adjusted_for_contrast`, `least_mix_clearing`, a closure-parameterized 24-step bisection with exactly one production caller (line 1112, the `muted` colour). A fixed 1/16-step loop toward the opposite pole is about ten lines. ~65 lines.
- `render.rs:2020-2059` — `task_detail`'s plain branch, a second full layout of the same `detail_rows` beside `task_detail_card`. One layout with ASCII glyph substitution covers both. ~40 lines. Defence on record: byte-stable output for pipes, scripts and docs examples — check that before merging the two.
- `render.rs:2233-2256` — 12 of `DetailField`'s 22 variants are never matched anywhere; both layouts route them through `_ =>`. Collapse to one `Plain`. ~12 lines.
- `theme.rs:452-461` — `Style::dim()` and `Style::underline()`, both `#[allow(dead_code)]`, with callers only inside `mod tests`. The `dim`/`underline` fields stay: `spec_d` and mono's `overdue` set them. ~10 lines.
- `render.rs:2638-2648` — `fit_facts`, a 10-line wrapper over `keep_ranked` + `join("   ")` with one caller (`next_task`, render.rs:3891), and the echo has its own unrelated function of the same name. Inline it. ~10 lines.
- `docs/obj_ref.rs:575-586` — re-declared urgency weights (`PRIORITY_TERMS`, `DUE_RAMP_DAYS`, `AGE_PER_DAY`, `AGE_CAP`) plus a guard test holding them to the engine. Export them as consts from `tasqx_core::urgency`, which has them as inline literals at `urgency.rs:79`. ~12 lines.
- `docs/api_ref.rs:783-785` — `describe_cached` uses `Box::leak` on every description to fabricate `&'static str` for `Param<'static>`. Make `Param` hold `Cow<'_, str>`. ~5 lines.
- `render.rs:4197-4215` — `tail_fit`'s manual reverse char walk into a `Vec<char>`. `unicode-truncate` is already a dependency and used by `truncate` directly above; it ships `unicode_truncate_start`. ~12 lines.

Note for sizing: render.rs is 9,025 lines but only 4,223 are production — `mod tests` opens at render.rs:4256.

existing.title: Collapse the duplicated engine, token-parser and markdown helpers in core
existing.description:
tasqx-core carries a set of small duplications that each looked reasonable alone: the same context struct built by hand in four places, the same grouping match in two reports, four copies of `home_dir()` spelled three different ways, five functions for relative-time prose, two near-identical OTEL parsers, and the ten-file engine roster spelled out four times so four separate hand-rolled source scanners can read it. This task collapses them, about 700 lines, with no change to any answer the engine gives. Done means the conformance, engine, tokens and memory suites pass untouched and the four gates are green.

Cut list (from the repo-wide ponytail audit, 2026-09-17):
- `engine/undo.rs:130-294` — `NOT_UNDOABLE`, a three-to-five sentence prose paragraph for each of 20 non-undoable ops. One clause per op naming the sanctioned inverse verb, one table line each. ~150 lines. Defence on record: the refusal must name what does take it back — keep that property, drop the essay.

existing.title: tasqx board, phase 1: read-only live kanban in the browser
existing.description:
A kanban board in the browser that shows every task in its state column, updates live as tasks change, and writes nothing. It matters because users asked to see the state of the backlog at a glance without a terminal, and a read-only first phase proves the transport and the security boundary before any drag can mutate the store. Done means: `tasqx board` opens the page in the default browser, the five columns fill from the store, and a change made from the CLI or MCP appears on the page without a reload.

Design mockup (interactive, the agreed look and behaviour): https://claude.ai/artifact/JwknrebxJoXvpMqcmgh3SX

Shape, ruled in conversation 2026-09-16:
- `tasqx board` is a new CLI verb in crates/tasqx-cli. It spawns or joins the daemon (serve.rs, `run_daemon`) and serves ONE self-contained HTML page over loopback HTTP, the same idiom as `report --html` (html.rs) and `tasqx docs` (docs.rs): inline CSS, inline script, system font stack, no CDN, no bundler, no framework. Vanilla JS, Pointer Events for drag in phase 2.
- Transport: extend the daemon's existing loopback HTTP reader (the OTLP receiver in crates/tasqx-core/src/otlp.rs binds 127.0.0.1 only) rather than adding a web framework. Routes: `/` the page, `/api` proxies JSON API envelopes 1:1 (same envelope as `tasqx api`), `/events` streams daemon `task.changed` pushes as Server-Sent Events.
- Security from day one: bind 127.0.0.1 only, never 0.0.0.0; check the `Origin` header on every request; require a per-launch random token (in the URL on open, then a cookie). DESIGN.md §7 already says a network transport must carry its own peer authentication and must not reuse the MCP scope as an auth boundary.
- Columns are the states the core already derives, each header showing its filter expression: Backlog `status:backlog`, Blocked `@blocked`, Ready `@working`, Active `status:active` (one at a time, D6), Done `completed.after:-7d`. Sort within a column is urgency, the same absolute scale and three bands as `list` (D119); the card carries the D117 rail glyph (▶ active, ⊘ blocked), priority folded into the urgency gauge, due as a calendar day, tags, blocked-by, checks progress and note count.
- Swimlanes: none, by project, by priority. Search box filters title, tags, notes and id.
- Palette generated from the active tasqx theme as html.rs already does; light and dark both.
- Not in this phase: any write. The page renders fully without the event stream and shows "daemon · offline" when it drops.

existing.title: tasqx board, phase 2: drag to start, stop, done, cancel and set priority
existing.description:
Dragging a card between columns changes the task through the same API verbs every other surface uses, and dropping it on a priority zone sets H, M or L. It matters because this is the request users made: set state and priority by dragging instead of typing. Done means: every drop in the mockup (https://claude.ai/artifact/JwknrebxJoXvpMqcmgh3SX) sends exactly one envelope with `expected_rev`, a conflict re-fetches the card and says so, and a toast names what happened in the verb's own words with Undo.

Drop semantics, ruled 2026-09-16:
- to Active: `task.start` (displaces the running task per D6; the toast says what was stopped and after how long)
- to Done: `task.done` (toast lists `unblocked`)
- to Ready from Active: `task.stop`; from Done: `task.reopen`; from Backlog: `task.modify {wait:null, scheduled:null}`
- to Backlog: `task.modify {wait:+1w}` (a week is the placeholder; the card panel holds the real date)
- to Blocked: refused with a toast. Blocked is derived from dependencies and is not a drop target.
- Priority tray (H / M / L / clear) appears under the cursor while dragging; drop sends `task.modify {priority}`. Priority is the only draggable ordering: within-column order stays urgency. NO manual rank field in this phase, and record the ruling in DESIGN.md §12: a free-form rank is a schema change, a sync question and a second ordering principle fighting urgency. If users still want it later, a rank that feeds the urgency formula is the version that does not split the model.
- Keys mirror the dashboard: j/k move, s start, d done, enter open, / search, esc close.
- Every write passes `expected_rev` read from the card's cached `_rev`; on `conflict` the page re-fetches that task and toasts "another session changed it (rev N)".
- Undo in the toast calls `undo` for the last write (the CLI's `tasqx undo`).
- Ships `/api` write proxying behind the same Origin check and per-launch token as phase 1; a `--scope read` flag on `tasqx board` serves the page with writes disabled, matching `mcp serve`.

existing.title: store.import renumbers a task whose short_id another task in the destination already holds, instead of refusing
existing.description: Exporting from one machine and importing into another machine's live store fails with exit 5 whenever a payload task carries a short_id that a different task already holds there. The refusal message in crates/tasqx-core/src/engine/transfer.rs (the D4 guard before the task upsert) says "import into a fresh store, or renumber", but no renumber exists. Since the real key is the UUIDv7 id and short_id is a display handle no other table references (dependencies, annotations, checks, links and events all key on id; projects merge by name), the fix is to mint a fresh number for the incoming task rather than refuse. Decision: when the payload short_id belongs to a DIFFERENT id in the destination, keep the task's id, take a new short_id from alloc_short_id, and report each move in the response as `renumbered: [{id, from, to}]` so the caller can fix branch names and "#n" mentions. Before the loop, bump_short_id_floor to max(payload short_ids)+1 so a minted number can never collide with a later payload task. When the payload id already exists in the destination, the upsert keeps the destination's short_id instead of writing excluded.short_id, so a task renumbered on import survives a second round trip. Two payload tasks claiming one number stays a refusal: that document is incoherent everywhere. Done means: importing an export from store A into store B where both minted #1..#n merges every task with fresh numbers for the collisions, dependencies intact, and a repeat import of the same file changes nothing. No new flag; the response line names what moved.

existing.title: Installed tasqx is Homebrew and shadows ~/.cargo/bin; cargo install --force does not change what Claude Code launches
existing.body:
Ruling: on this machine the real `tasqx` is the Homebrew formula at /opt/homebrew/bin/tasqx, and /opt/homebrew/bin precedes ~/.cargo/bin on PATH. `cargo install --path crates/tasqx-cli --force` (the line CLAUDE.md recommends) lands in ~/.cargo/bin and is shadowed, so neither the shell nor Claude Code's MCP config (`claude mcp add tasqx -- tasqx mcp serve --scope write`, bare name) picks it up.

Why it matters: after 0.9.0 was cut the user was told to cargo-install to get the new initialize instructions; the result was two binaries and a shadowed one. A change in this tree reaches the user's sessions only after a release plus `brew upgrade tasqx`, or by pointing the MCP command at ~/.cargo/bin/tasqx explicitly.

How to apply: do not recommend cargo install to this user for trying a change; either release, or say the absolute-path MCP override and its cleanup. Verify with `which tasqx` and `tasqx --version` (the version line carries the commit hash and `-dirty`).

new.body:
Ruling (2026-09-15): the everyday `tasqx` on the dev machine is `cargo install --path crates/tasqx-cli --force` from this tree, at ~/.cargo/bin/tasqx. The Homebrew formula was uninstalled that day.

With both installed, /opt/homebrew/bin precedes ~/.cargo/bin on PATH, so the Homebrew copy silently shadowed the cargo build and the MCP server (configured as a bare `tasqx`) ran the released binary, not the tree.

How to apply: after merging anything under crates/, run the cargo install as CLAUDE.md says. Never `brew install tasqx` on this machine. A running Claude Code session keeps the old MCP process until restart.

existing.title: Timestamp text is never a sort key: order by UUIDv7 id where the id carries the instant (D142), normalise the stamp with rtrim 'Z' where it does not (D144)
existing.body:
Ruling: any ORDER BY (or Rust String cmp) over a tasqx timestamp column written by util::now() is wrong as written. Two correct forms:
- Order by the UUIDv7 id when the row is immutable and its id is its only instant: annotations (page, brief subqueries, export) and token_usage in D142; events since D59 (storage::event_id_floor).
- Order by `rtrim(<stamp>, 'Z')` when the stamp carries information the id does not: memory.list sorts `rtrim(modified, 'Z') DESC, id DESC` (D144), because `modified` moves on memory.update and on a memory.import replace-by-source (D143) and the surface promises newest-modified first (D115 #133, tasqx_list_memory description, docs/wiki/Memory.md). id DESC was proposed and rejected there: it would silently turn the browse into newest-created.

Why: util::now() is jiff Timestamp::to_string(), which prints a variable-length fractional second (trailing zeros trimmed, none at a whole second). Under SQLite BINARY collation (and Rust byte order) 'Z' > any digit > '.', so `10.12Z` > `10.123Z` and `10Z` > `10.9Z`: an older row sorts above a newer one. Stripping the terminator fixes it because a trimmed decimal fraction compares correctly as a plain prefix string (`10` < `10.9`, `10.12` < `10.123`, `10.2` > `10.12`). D142 surfaced as a v0.9.0 release failure on the aarch64-apple-darwin runner only; D144 as tests/memory.rs list_pages_newest_first_and_next_offset_walks_to_the_end failing once under whole-workspace load.

Still open: engine.rs compare_by sorts task.list's `created`/`modified` keys by String cmp, same defect (task #87) — use the same rtrim/trim_end_matches('Z') normalisation there.

Exception: otlp_samples.id is a UUIDv5 over a natural key (replay-idempotent) and carries no time, so it stays ORDER BY ts, id; its ts is exporter-supplied, not util::now().

Import preserves foreign annotation ids, so id order then reflects the origin store's clock, which is still correct.

Test pattern: add rows through the API so ids are v7-ordered, then UPDATE the stamp column with crafted stamps whose text order inverts write order (10Z, 10.1Z, 10.12Z, 10.123Z); see stamp_annotations in engine/task.rs tests and memory_list_orders_by_modified_instant_not_the_variable_length_text in engine/memory.rs tests.

new.title: Annotations are ordered by their UUIDv7 id, never by the `created` text (extends D59's ruling on events)
new.body:
**Decision:** every read that orders annotations orders by `id` alone — the page behind `task.get`, and so `tasqx show`; the two correlated subqueries that pick a prerequisite's newest note for `task.brief`; and the `store.export` relation. `created` is no longer a sort key anywhere, not even as the leading term with `id` as a tiebreak. The same rule applies to `token_usage`, whose `id` is minted the same way: `task.get`'s measurements, the export, the log-parse scan behind `tokens.recompute` and the channel-conflict probe all order by `id`.

**Why: the column cannot do the job, and a release run proved it.** `created` is TEXT written by `util::now` as a jiff `Timestamp`, which prints a *variable-length* fractional second — trailing zeros trimmed, the fraction omitted entirely at a whole second. Under SQLite's BINARY collation `'Z'` (0x5A) sorts above every digit and above `'.'`, so `...10.12Z` sorts above `...10.123Z` and `...10Z` above `...10.9Z`, and an older row lands above a newer one. This is not a new discovery: `storage::event_id_floor` already documents exactly this defect for `events.ts`, and D59 already settled that events are bounded and ordered by their UUIDv7 `id` for it. Annotations were simply never given the same treatment. The evidence arrived as a v0.9.0 release job failing on aarch64-apple-darwin and nowhere else: that runner is fast enough that a task's annotations land inside a single millisecond, so whichever of them happens to end in a zero digit gets its stamp trimmed and jumps the queue. A test that passes on three targets and fails on the fastest one is the shape this defect takes — the fault is in the query, and the slow machines were only hiding it.

**Why `id` is the right key and not merely a workaround.** It is UUIDv7, so it carries the creation instant in its high bits; `uuid`'s `now_v7` guarantees ordering within a process, which is where a burst of annotations comes from. It is unique, which `created` never was — several annotations genuinely share a timestamp, and a window whose tie order differs between two queries pages inconsistently, showing one row twice and skipping another. And it is already the PRIMARY KEY, so the order is index-served with no second index to write on every insert. `store.export` has ordered memory docs this way since D41 for the same reason. An import that carries foreign ids preserves them, so ordering then reflects the origin store's clock — which is the correct answer, since that is where those annotations were written.

**What does not change.** `created` remains the stored and displayed timestamp on every surface that shows one: it is still what `task.get`, `brief`, `show` and the export return, and still what a reader sees beside a note. Only the sort key moves. No schema change, no migration, and no response field added or removed — the rows come back in the same shape, in the order they were actually written.

existing.title: Every write door that changes a doc's text must move docs.rev: memory.add 0, memory.update cur+1, memory.import cur+1 (D143), store.import carries the export's rev
existing.body:
Ruling (D143, 2026-09-14): any route that rewrites a memory doc's title/body must bump docs.rev, because memory.update's expected_rev guard is a per-id promise, not a per-route one — a door that changes text without moving the counter makes the guard silently false for every caller.

How each door does it now: memory_add inserts rev 0; memory_update writes cur_rev + 1; memory_import looks up `SELECT id, rev FROM docs WHERE source` and binds cur_rev + 1 (or 0 for a new source) into the upsert with `rev=excluded.rev`; store.import writes the export's `_rev` verbatim. Convention: compute the new rev in Rust from a row read inside the same IMMEDIATE transaction (begin_mutation), then bind it — not `rev=rev+1` in SQL and not a read-back SELECT afterwards. A review rejected the SQL-side form as a third style in the crate.

Known gaps filed, not fixed: store.import's doc branch has no rewind guard like the task branch's #177 check (task #84); docs.source is not unique so import's replace lookup can pick an arbitrary row (task #85); a byte-identical re-import still bumps rev and counts as replaced, pending a ruling (task #86). When adding a new door that touches doc text, add the bump and extend the conformance shape if the response carries `_rev`.

new.title: A memory.import that replaces a doc by source bumps its rev, so a stale expected_rev conflicts instead of clobbering the import (extends #135's guard to the import door)
new.body:
**Decision:** `memory.import`'s replace-by-source UPDATE now writes `rev` alongside `source`, `title`, `body`, `search_body` and `modified`: the matched row's rev plus one, read by the same lookup that finds the row and bound into the upsert the way `memory.update` and `store.import` already do it. The per-doc entry in the `memory.import` result carries `_rev`, and the `memory.add` event it writes (`via: "memory.import"`) records `rev` — both additive to the existing shape. A fresh insert (no matching `source`) still starts at rev 0.

**Why:** `memory.update`'s `expected_rev` exists so a writer who read a doc at rev N cannot overwrite a change it never saw (task #135). A re-import after the file changed on disk is exactly such a change, but the upsert's SET list left `rev` untouched, so a doc re-imported to v2 still answered rev 0, and an `update` pinned to the rev-0 it read before the import sailed through the guard and replaced v2 with stale text. Found by the September 2026 test audit (task #67). The other import door, `store.import` in `engine/transfer.rs`, already carries `rev` in its SET list, so the two doors disagreed on a promise the guard is supposed to make absolute. Bumping from the row the lookup found (the lookup and the upsert share one IMMEDIATE transaction, so nothing can move it between them) keeps the counter monotonic for the id at this door, which is exactly what `expected_rev` compares against; the export/import door's own rewind gap is tracked separately (task #84).

**Why not leave import out of the guard's reach:** rejected because the guard's promise is per-id, not per-route — a door that changes the text without moving the counter makes "your `expected_rev` protects you" false for every caller of `memory.update`, not just the one who happened to re-import.

**What does not change.** id and `created` still survive a source-replace (#178, #198). The row is still reached with `ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE`, never DELETE+INSERT (D41). No schema change, no migration. `memory.update`'s own rev bump and its `conflict` error shape are unchanged. `store.import`'s doc branch wrote `rev` from the payload all along, but carried no floor on it until task #84 closed the gap this decision's "Why" paragraph flagged: it now refuses a doc whose payload `_rev` is behind what the store already holds, the same `stored > rev` conflict its task branch (#177) already returned, so restoring an older export can no longer rewind a doc's rev and reopen this decision's own guard.

**Amended by D221.** A re-import whose title and body (and named project) already match the stored doc is no revision: rev, `modified` and the event log stay put, and the doc is reported `unchanged`, not `replaced`. Only a replace that changes something bumps rev as written here.

existing.title: Task card rendering: box card is a document, rail card is a screen; Description comes from the oldest annotation (D146)
existing.body:
Ruling: a task has two human renderings and they are not interchangeable. The CLI rail card (render.rs task_detail_card, D76/D117) is a SCREEN: terminal width, theme paint, PLAIN under a pipe. The box card (markdown::task_card, D146) is a DOCUMENT: fixed 72 cells per line, Unicode or ASCII borders as a parameter, no paint, byte-identical wherever printed. Reach it with `view: "card"` on tasqx_get_task / tasqx_brief_task (fenced ```text) or `tasqx show|brief <ref> --card [--ascii]`. `--card` ignores caps.unicode on purpose: theme.rs detect_from returns Caps::PLAIN for any pipe, and piping the card into a document is the use.

Description row: first paragraph of the OLDEST annotation on the page; Delivered (closed tasks): first paragraph of the NEWEST. No `description` column — rejected because it would be a schema change, a frozen conformance row (D56), CLI sugar and an MCP param for text the first annotation already carries. Convention that follows: open a task's first annotation with one plain-language paragraph, and open the final annotation with a plain-language summary.

Geometry lives in three constants in markdown.rs (CARD_WIDTH 72, label text 11, value text 54) tied by a const assert; every cell is measured with unicode-width, never len(); `cell()`+`fit()` re-measure the assembled line as the last defence against grapheme clusters the wrapper miscounts. Card-only time formatting: durations always compact (`4h`), Both → date + relative with no UTC clock (house style §3). If the card ever wraps its border, look at those helpers before the wrapper.

new.title: A task has two human renderings: the rail card is a screen, the box card is a document (extends D49, D76)
new.body:
**Decision:** `markdown::task_card` renders one task as a fixed 72-column box-drawn card, pure like `task_detail` (D49): no clock, no environment, no theme; `now` and the time format arrive in `CardOpts`, and the borders are a parameter (`Borders::Unicode` or `Borders::Ascii`). Every line is exactly 72 display cells, measured with `unicode-width`, wrapped at words and broken inside a word only when the word itself is wider than the cell. The MCP tools `tasqx_get_task` and `tasqx_brief_task` take `view: "markdown" | "card"` (default `markdown`, a transport-only argument beside `include_json`); under `card` the rendered block is the card inside a ```text fence and everything about the JSON block — its default presence, D66's budget steps — is unchanged. The CLI prints the same bytes under `tasqx show <ref> --card` and `tasqx brief <ref> --card`, Unicode borders regardless of `caps.unicode`, `--ascii` for the fallback borders, never painted. The default outputs of both tools and both verbs are byte-identical to before.

**Why a second card, not a second use of the first.** The CLI already had a card — D76's rail card under the D117 house style — and this is not a second one for the same purpose. The rail card is a SCREEN: it is fitted to the terminal's width, painted by the theme, and carries the rail glyphs; piped, it degrades to the plain ledger (`Caps::PLAIN`) because a screen has no meaning off a terminal. The box card is a DOCUMENT: a block that means the same thing pasted into a chat reply, a pull request or a report, which requires fixed geometry and no escape codes. Two renderings for two destinations is D49's one-rendering-per-reader rule, not an exception to it: the reader of the rail card is a person at a terminal; the reader of the box card is a person reading a document an agent wrote, and D49's own markdown table serves the third reader, the model.

**Why the Description row has no column of its own.** The store has no plain-language description column; a task's context lives in its annotations (checks carry criteria, annotations carry prose — D138). The card takes the first paragraph of the OLDEST annotation on the page as the description and, on a closed task, the first paragraph of the NEWEST as what was delivered. Adding a `description` column instead would have been a schema change, a new frozen conformance row (D56), CLI sugar and an MCP parameter, all to carry text the first annotation already holds and the same author writes either way. The convention this fixes is stated where agents read it (the tasqx-workflow skill): open a task's first annotation with one plain-language paragraph. When the oldest annotation is not on the page (`annotations_offset + shown < annotations_total`), the row says so rather than showing the wrong note.

**Why `--card` ignores `caps.unicode`.** The capability answers "what can this terminal draw" and a document is not drawn on this terminal: `tasqx show 42 --card | pbcopy` is the use, and `detect_from` returns `Caps::PLAIN` for exactly that pipe. `--ascii` is the explicit fallback for the one destination (a legacy console, a plain-text mail) that cannot show the box characters.

**What does not change.** No schema change, no new response field, no frozen result altered; `task_detail`, `task_brief` and the CLI's rail card and ledger are byte-identical; the D66 budget logic runs over whichever renderer the caller chose.

existing.title: Codebase indexing in tasqx: not built; ripwire maps code live, tasqx memory checks its own freshness on demand
existing.body:
Ruling (2026-09-21, plan memory-freshness, tasks #787-#795, all landed; DESIGN.md D178, D180, D182): tasqx does not index source code. A code mapper on PATH (ripwire, github.com/redhat-et/ripwire, Apache-2.0, C++23; 0.6.1 has an incremental cache, 0.2s warm, --json, --mcp, --index-out) answers where-is-X, callers and impact live, so a symbol index inside tasqx would be a second, staler copy. What tasqx built instead is freshness for the memory it already owns: memory import records origin_path, origin_mtime, origin_size on the docs row (D180); `tasqx memory import --refresh` (API memory.refresh) re-imports changed files and reports missing ones without deleting; every doc hit from memory.search and task.brief carries stale:true|false|null; MCP initialize runs the sweep under a write scope and says so in one instructions line. mtime+size is the fast filter, an exact title-and-body compare is the truth, so a touch is not a change.

ripwire is not bundled and not auto-installed (D178): tasqx setup, initialize, install.sh and install.ps1 only say whether it is on PATH and point at the upstream repository URL. Upstream ships release tarballs for linux/macos only, no Homebrew formula, no Scoop manifest, no Windows build; hosting a formula in homebrew-tasqx was declined (hint only).

Why not the rest:
- No symbol index in tasqx: tree-sitter per language, incremental parsing and a call graph are ripwire's whole product; tasqx is the organiser (DESIGN.md line 3), and D41 lexical ranking would let symbol noise drown rulings (brief already reserves slots for rulings, task #95).
- No importing ripwire's map as memory docs: same drowning, plus it goes stale between imports while ripwire itself does not.
- No background watcher or daemon timer: D74 is retiring the daemon, `notify` is not a dependency, and a stat per doc at initialize plus a stat per returned hit is exact and costs milliseconds; a watcher runs for its whole life to save that.
- No brief-time shell-out to ripwire from tasqx: couples a product surface to a third-party binary; the agent runs ripwire itself in 0.2s after the brief.
- No path-aware memory search ("what touched engine/memory.rs"): FTS already tokenises paths; revisit only if a search on a file name proves noisy.

The scanning the user saw happened in subagents (1337:scout, 1337:builder) handed Grep and Read with no map-first instruction; fixed in the 1337-claude plugin (#793, landed).

new.title: Memory freshness is checked on demand against the origin file, never watched; source code is mapped live by an external tool, never indexed in tasqx (task #792; extends D41, D74, D178, D179, D180)
new.body:
**Decision:** two rulings, recorded together because they are the same principle answered on either side of one boundary — what tasqx stores versus what it defers to a tool that already does the job live. On memory: an imported doc's `origin_path`, `origin_mtime` and `origin_size` are recorded once, at `memory.import` (D180). Checking freshness never re-reads a file on its own initiative; it happens on demand, at three doors — `tasqx memory import --refresh`, a write-scoped MCP `initialize`, and every hit `memory.search` or `task.brief` returns — and each does the same two-step check: mtime and size against what the filesystem answers now is the fast filter, and only a mismatch opens the file for the truth, an exact compare of the freshly read title and body against what is stored, so a `touch` with no byte changed is not reported as one. `--refresh` and `initialize` re-read and land what changed, bump `rev`, and name what they could not find under `missing` without deleting it — the file may be off this machine, not gone from the world. A hit instead carries `stale: true`, told and left for the reader to act on, because a search is not the door that writes.

Source code gets the opposite answer: tasqx does not index it. A code mapper already on the operator's `PATH` — ripwire, D178 — answers where a symbol is defined, who calls it and what a change would touch, live and per invocation. A symbol index kept inside tasqx would be a second copy of that answer, staler the moment either tool runs again, and its symbol-name traffic would win ranking slots under D41's lexical BM25 that a stored ruling should have held.

**Why:** a stat call per imported doc at a session's `initialize` and per hit a search or brief actually returns costs milliseconds and is exact, because the filesystem already answers it for free — the same fact D180's decision leaned on. A watcher or a daemon timer would run for the whole life of a process to save that one stat, at the moment D74 is retiring the daemon tasqx already has; `notify` is not a dependency this project carries or is adding one for. The same shape answers the code question: ripwire's own incremental cache is the live index, kept warm by the tool that owns the language grammars, and tasqx re-deriving a weaker copy of it buys staleness, not currency.

**Rejected: importing a code map as memory docs.** It goes stale the moment either tasqx or the mapper runs again, on the store's own clock rather than the file's — the exact drift `origin_path` exists to detect for prose, and a symbol dump has no comparable "unchanged" fast path. **Rejected: a brief-time shell-out to the mapper from tasqx.** It couples a product surface to a third-party binary's presence and exit code; the agent already runs the mapper itself in the time a stat takes. **Rejected: a path-aware memory search** ("what touched `engine/memory.rs`"). FTS5 already tokenises a path's segments, so a plain query finds it; a second parameter for what the existing one already answers is drift D30 would name.

existing.title: MCP initialize instructions field: cross-tool workflow is in-band, per-tool contract stays on the description (D141 amends D75)
existing.body:
Ruling: `initialize` answers `instructions` with a scope-aware workflow nudge (search before deciding, track multi-step work as tasks, brief/start/annotate/complete, store decisions with the why, import docs on day one, always `tasqx <verb>`). D75's refusal to put per-tool content (the modify retry protocol) into `instructions` still stands; only cross-tool guidance goes there.

Why: a tool description is read after the agent has already chosen the tool, so nothing on a description can say "reach for tasqx at all". `instructions` is the one in-band field hosts (Claude Code, Cursor) inject into the system prompt before any tool is chosen. Before this, a fresh install had no in-band nudge and the starter-prompt guide said so.

Why scope-aware: under `--scope` read the write tools are absent from tools/list, so naming one would make the refusal the agent's first hint about the scope. The read variant names no write tool, says the server is read-only once, and tells the agent to put what it would have stored into its reply.

Guard: tests in crates/tasqx-core/tests/mcp.rs bind every `tasqx_*` name in both variants to `tool_roster()`, so a tool rename reddens the build. If you edit the text, keep tool names exact and keep write tools out of READ_ONLY.

Gotcha: the docs page `page_mcp` captures a real initialize response and elides the field with sed; the snippet is not executed by tests, so re-check it by hand when the response shape changes.

new.title: initialize carries a scope-aware instructions block: the workflow is in-band, the per-tool contract stays on the description (amends D75)
new.body:
**Decision:** `initialize` now answers `instructions` with a condensed workflow: search before deciding; track multi-step work as tasks; brief, start, annotate, complete; store decisions with their why; import on day one; `tasqx <verb>`, never a bare `tasqx`. The text is built from `Scope`: the read-only variant names no write tool and tells the agent to hand the user what it could not store, rather than pretending the store took it. A test binds every `tasqx_*` name the text uses to the live tool roster, so the block cannot drift out from under a rename the way prose elsewhere could.

**Why this amends rather than reverses D75.** D75 refused `instructions` for the `modify` retry protocol, and that refusal stands: nothing per-tool moves into `instructions`, because that content is read at the moment of choosing the tool and the description is what sits there. What D75 could not answer is the question that comes before any tool is chosen at all — whether to reach for tasqx in the first place. A fresh install exposed a roster of well-described tools and nothing said when, so the default agent behaviour was to keep its own in-conversation todo list; `docs/guides/agent-starter-prompt.md` said as much in its own opening paragraph. `instructions` is the only in-band field read before a tool is picked, and hosts including Claude Code and Cursor inject it straight into the system prompt — which makes it the one place a cross-tool nudge can live at all.

**Why scope-aware.** A read-only session told flatly to annotate would either fail loudly on every write attempt or, worse, drop the note silently. The read-only variant instead says once that the server is read-only and routes the content into the reply — the same rule the paste-anywhere starter prompt already gives an agent that finds `tasqx_add_memory` and `tasqx_annotate_task` missing from its tool list, now said by the server itself rather than left to a file the agent may never have been given.

**What stays out.** No `prompts` or `resources` capability is added alongside it; `instructions` is a nudge toward the workflow, not the workflow itself. The paste-anywhere block and the repo's own skill remain the fuller version — the reasons behind each rule, and the placeholders an operator tunes — for hosts that ignore `instructions` or truncate it. *Amended by D157: the session's standing rulings follow the workflow text.*

existing.title: Browser kanban board: a client of the JSON API over loopback HTTP, priority by drop zone, no manual rank
existing.body:
Ruling (2026-09-16): the browser kanban board (`tasqx board`, tasks #637 #638 #639) is one more client of the JSON API, served as a single self-contained HTML page over loopback HTTP from the daemon, with Server-Sent Events for live updates. It follows the `report --html` / `tasqx docs` idiom: inline CSS and script, no CDN, no framework, no bundler.

Why: DESIGN.md §2 says every surface, GUI included, is a client of the one API; the daemon already pushes `task.changed` and already runs a loopback HTTP reader (otlp.rs), so the board needs no new core method and no web framework.

Columns are the derived states with their filter expressions as headers (status:backlog, @blocked, @working, status:active, completed.after:-7d). Drags map to the existing verbs (task.start/stop/done/reopen/modify); Blocked is derived from dependencies and is not a drop target. Priority is set by dropping on an H/M/L zone. Within-column order stays urgency: NO manual rank field. Reason: a free-form rank is a schema change, a sync question, and a second ordering principle fighting urgency; if ever wanted, a rank that feeds the urgency formula is the version that does not split the model.

Security is part of phase 1, not later: 127.0.0.1 only, Origin header checked, per-launch token; DESIGN.md §7 already requires a network transport to carry its own peer authentication rather than reuse the MCP scope.

Phasing agreed by the user: 1 read-only live board, 2 drags and priority, 3 in-card edits.

new.title: `tasqx board` is a loopback, token-gated, Origin-checked browser kanban that reads through the daemon, on an HTTP reader it shares with the OTLP receiver (task #637; phase 1 of #637, #638, #639)
new.body:
**Decision.** `tasqx board` serves one self-contained page and two routes from `tasqx_core::board`, a listener beside `otlp` on a shared `tasqx_core::http` reader and writer (the request parser, the header and body caps, the whole-request deadline and the response writer were lifted out of `otlp.rs`, which keeps its own accept loop and policy). **(a) Bind** is `127.0.0.1` and `Board::bind` refuses any non-loopback address; port `0` (a free port) by default, `board.port` or `--port` to fix one. **(b) Token** is 32 random bytes as hex: `/?token=…` is traded for an `HttpOnly; SameSite=Strict` cookie named for the port and redirects to `/`; every other request needs the cookie, compared in constant time. A free port gets a fresh token each run and writes nothing; a fixed port keeps its token in `board-token` beside `config.toml`, owner-only (0600), so a bookmark survives a restart. **(c) Host and Origin** are checked on every request before anything is revealed: `Host` must be `127.0.0.1:<port>` or `localhost:<port>` (DNS rebinding), and an `Origin`, when sent, must be the board's own (CSRF). **(d) Phase 1 is read-only by construction:** `POST /api` forwards an envelope only for the methods in `board::READ_METHODS` (`task.list`, `task.get`, `project.list`), default deny, so a write added to the API later is unreachable until someone lists it; every other HTTP method is a 405. **(e) `/events` is server-sent events**: a `daemon` event naming whether the daemon is reachable, then each `task.changed` push as it arrives, with a heartbeat; the page repaints from `task.list` and shows "daemon · offline" when the stream drops. **(f) The page** is inline CSS and one nonce'd inline script, palette from the active theme as `report --html` does, and the listener's CSP (`default-src 'none'`, `connect-src 'self'`) makes "no external request" a browser-enforced fact. **(g) Not an authentication system:** the board is single-user and local; behind a reverse proxy, authentication is the proxy's job; there are no accounts, roles or multi-user sync. It needs a running daemon, like `watch`, and does not spawn one. A pinned `TASQX_NOW` refuses it, as it refuses `watch` (D149).

**Seams left for #638 and #639.** Writes arrive by adding methods to `READ_METHODS`' successor under a `--scope read|write` switch mirroring `mcp serve`, with `actor = board` on every write, behind the same token and Origin checks; the page's `api()` helper is the one call site that would send them. Cards carry no checks or note counts because `task.list` does not return them; the detail panel reads them from `task.get`.

**Why.** Loopback is not a user boundary on a shared host, and any web page can make a browser send a request to `127.0.0.1`, so the token is the boundary and Host plus Origin are the guard against the page being the attacker. The OTLP receiver and the board stay separate listeners because their threat models differ: one is unauthenticated telemetry ingress, off by default; the other authenticates and holds connections open. A read allowlist rather than a write denylist is the only form that stays safe as the API grows.

**Rejected: a web framework** (blocking threads on loopback are enough, §2's runtime-free rule). **Rejected: the token in the URL on every request** (it leaks through history and `Referer`; the cookie is set once and the URL cleaned). **Rejected: spawning a daemon from `board`** (nothing else auto-spawns one, and a daemon the board started would outlive it).

existing.title: Desktop first release: scope, platforms, unsigned artifacts and standing permission for the autonomous build
existing.body:
Ruling (owner, 2026-09-19): build Tasqx Desktop (#689–#695 plus #741) autonomously to a first running version on macOS, Windows and Linux; the release is unsigned with build-it-yourself instructions; the agent has standing permission for every decision the build needs.

Scope: #689 shell + design system, #690 graph.query API, #691 dashboard, #692 memory explorer, #693 graph, #694 editing + daemon events, #741 charts (DAG, treemap, CFD, optional Sky 3D) — all in. Recommended order: vertical slice #689 → #690 → #691, then a look from the owner, then the rest.

Platforms: all three from #689 onward; macOS verified locally, Windows and Linux through CI runners.

Signing: none for the first release. #695 closes with unsigned artifacts plus docs/maintainers instructions for local builds and for the maintainer-run signing/notarization step; the tag workflow names the secrets and passes without them. The owner tests the unsigned build first.

Standing permission (beyond the CLAUDE.md merge rule): add GitHub workflows, add npm dependencies, make design-system and UX choices without per-screen sign-off. Each such choice is recorded in the task's annotation so the owner can veto afterwards — "first running version, tweak later".

Why: the owner wants a usable app in hand before polishing to taste, and does not want to be asked per screen. Not in the repo: D160 (DESIGN.md) freezes the architecture but says nothing about signing policy, #741's inclusion, or how much the agent may decide alone.

new.title: Tasqx Desktop's first release is unsigned and has no updater: a version tag reads the signing secrets and passes without them, no desktop workflow publishes, and an opt-in notice says when a newer release exists (task #695; amends D160, applies D10)
new.body:
**Decision:** D160's "protected version tags alone produce signed/notarized artifacts, failing if the named signing secrets are absent" becomes: a `v*` tag is the only run that reads the signing secrets, and it **passes** when they are absent, uploading the same unsigned bundles a pull request does. `.github/workflows/desktop.yml` builds macOS, Windows and Linux bundles on pull requests, pushes to `main`, `v*` tags and dispatch, and uploads them as workflow artifacts; none of its jobs is a required check. The secrets it names are `APPLE_CERTIFICATE`, `APPLE_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD`, `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY`, `APPLE_ID`, `APPLE_PASSWORD`, `APPLE_TEAM_ID`, `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE` and `WINDOWS_CERTIFICATE_PASSWORD`; off a tag every one is forced empty. One script, `scripts/desktop-bundle.sh`, is both CI's build step and the maintainer's local signing command: it treats an empty variable as unset, signs each platform it finds an identity for and leaves the rest unsigned. Unsigned macOS bundles are ad-hoc signed (`bundle.macOS.signingIdentity: "-"`), so `codesign --verify --deep --strict` passes on them; `APPLE_SIGNING_IDENTITY` overrides it. The workflow's token is `contents: read` and no step tags or creates a release, so it cannot publish; `release.yml` stays the only workflow that does.

**No updater (D10 stands).** D160's "opt-in signature-verified updates" and "rollback" are withdrawn for the desktop app as they stand for the CLI: the app never downloads or installs anything itself, and carries no Tauri updater, no updater key and no update endpoint. What it does instead is D10's passive note: with **Check for a newer release** switched on in Settings (off by default, because it is the one request the app makes on its own, §10), it asks `api.github.com/repos/dimitritholen/tasqx/releases/latest` once at start-up and, when that tag is newer than the app's version, shows a dismissible notice linking the release page (`src/shell/updates.ts`, `UpdateNotice.tsx`). Offline it does not reach the network; any failure is no notice. The host's only new command, `open_release_page`, opens plain URLs under the repository's releases path and nothing else. Going back a version is reinstalling the previous bundle; the data lives in the tasqx store, not the app.

**Release checks.** `scripts/desktop-release-check.sh` checks one version across the workspace, the app and a tag (`scripts/bump-version.sh --apply` now writes the app's five version sites), that this host's bundles exist, the release smoke suite (`src/test/integration/release.test.tsx`: the whole app against a real daemon on a disposable, deliberately downgraded store, asserting it never dialled anything but the scratch socket), and an install, launch, connect, quit and clean uninstall of the bundle. The desktop workflow runs it on all three runners.

Local build and signing steps: `docs/maintainers/desktop-release.md`.

**Why.** The owner ruled (2026-09-19, restated 2026-10-08) that the first desktop release ships unsigned and that the owner tests that build before signing becomes its own task; a tag run that failed without secrets would make every tag red until identities are bought. Forcing the secrets empty off a tag keeps "only a tag signs" true for pull requests from branches of this repository, which GitHub does give secrets to. The owner ruled on 2026-10-08 that D10 holds for the desktop app too: a release notice, never a self-update.

**Rejected:** a second tag-only workflow (it would duplicate the whole build matrix and drift from it); failing on a partial set of secrets (an unsigned platform is the stated default, and the script's `off` lines say which one); the Tauri updater plugin (D10); `tauri-plugin-opener` for the one link (it pulled a newer `tauri` into the lockfile; a fixed-prefix host command is smaller); an update check on by default (§10's no phone-home).
